english: God, then, having His own Word internal within His own bowels, begot Him, emitting Him along with His own wisdom before all things.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF, 1885); Greek: Migne text, no named translator

what_it_says: God, having the Word endiathetos (immanent) in his own bowels, begot him, uttering (exereuxamenos) him together with his own Wisdom before all things.
limits: Dods renders endiathetos 'internal' and ekpheresthai-type verb 'emitting'; the Greek verb is ἐξερεύγομαι (utter/belch forth). The text gives a temporal-looking sequence (immanent, then begotten 'before all things') and names Wisdom in the same act; it does not say 'eternally' or 'from the substance of the Father'. Arian/Unitarian readers take 'begot' plus 'before all things' as a beginning of the Word; the answer must rest on other passages (see U3-14, U3-15, U3-17).

limits: The phrase 'ἐνδιάθετον ἐν καρδίᾳ Θεοῦ' (the brief's 'ever innate in the heart of God') is in 2.22, NOT 2.10. 'Πρὸ γὰρ τοῦ τι γίνεσθαι' (before anything came to be) is temporal-sounding; the 'counsellor' (σύμβουλος) and 'mind and thought' (νοῦς καὶ φρόνησις) are the brief's item 4.

what_it_says: The Word, being God and produced from God, is sent by the Father to a place whenever the Father wills, and is heard and seen there.
limits: The Word is called 'Θεὸς' without the article (predicate use, as in John 1:1 quoted at U3-16). The sending/location language is the passage a subordinationist or Unitarian reader cites; the text says the Word is 'sent' by the Father and 'found in a place'. Dods's 'naturally produced' translates πεφυκώς (produced/born from), not a term for homoousios.

english: But when God wished to make all that He determined on, He begot this Word, uttered, the first-born of all creation, not Himself being emptied of the Word [Reason], but having begotten Reason, and always conversing with His Reason.
translator: Marcus Dods (ANF, 1885); Greek: Migne text, no named translator

what_it_says: When God willed to make what he had determined, he begot this uttered Word, firstborn of all creation, without himself being emptied of the Word, and always conversed with his Word.
limits: Key Arian-type clause: 'πρωτότοκον πάσης κτίσεως' (firstborn of all creation) plus 'προφορικόν' (uttered) in a temporal frame ('when God wished'). The Theophilus answer is in the same sentence: 'οὐ κενωθεὶς αὐτὸς τοῦ λόγου, ἀλλὰ Λόγον γεννήσας' (not emptied of the Word, but begetting a Word). The text gives an analogy of utterance, not an account of eternal generation. Dods's '[Reason]' is his gloss for λόγος.

what_it_says: Theophilus quotes John 1:1 ('In the beginning was the Word; the Word was with God'), says that at first God was alone with the Word in him, then quotes 'The Word was God'.
limits: Theophilus explicitly cites John 1:1 with the Word 'in Him' before creation, and 'God' anarthrous for the Word. Limits: 'God was alone and the Word in him' is the sentence Unitarians read against a distinct Word before creation; the text says nothing about 'eternal' or 'consubstantial'. The English 'John 1:1' is Dods's reference insertion.

what_it_says: The voice is nothing but the Word of God, who is also his Son; this is not the mythic 'sons of gods begotten from intercourse' but the Word as truth describes him.
limits: 'Υἱὸς' (Son) appears here for the Word; it is one of the few Son-references in Book II (I did not count the whole work, so the brief's 'rarely says Son' is not tested here). The text rejects a mythic generation by intercourse, which bears on the 'begotten' objection. No 'homoousios' and no 'eternal' language in this sentence.
